title: Piano Trio No. 2 in E-flat major
hook: Schubert’s last year, a trio on a symphonic scale, and a slow march built on a Swedish song about the setting sun.

painting.title: A Town at Sunset
painting.pairingNote: A Swedish painter’s evening light over a quiet town and a path by the water; the slow movement’s tune comes from a Swedish song that begins “See, the sun is sinking”.

facts: Schubert wrote it in Vienna in 1827, the year of *Winterreise*; his title page reads “Nov. 1827, Op. 100”. He was thirty and had a year to live. It is the second of two large piano trios from those months, darker and more dramatic than the first, in B-flat.

The slow movement grew from a Swedish song, *Se solen sjunker* (“See, the sun is sinking”), which Schubert heard sung by the Swedish tenor Isak Albert Berg at the home of his friends the Fröhlich sisters.

Its official premiere was the centrepiece of the only public concert Schubert ever gave of his own music, on 26 March 1828, the first anniversary of Beethoven’s death, in the hall of Vienna’s Musikverein. The players were Carl Maria von Bocklet (piano), Joseph Michael Böhm (violin) and Joseph Linke (cello). The concert was a success, but the press barely noticed: Paganini’s first Vienna concert, three days later, swept everything else aside.

Before sending it to the Leipzig publisher Probst, Schubert cut about a hundred bars from the finale and its repeat, and asked that “the cuts marked in the last piece are to be most strictly observed”. The trio appeared in late 1828, just after his death in November; he probably never saw a printed copy. Asked whom it should be dedicated to, he replied: to no one, except those who find pleasure in it.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a bold opening on a large scale (I), a slow, walking lament (II), a light dance in canon (III), a long, restless finale where the slow movement’s song comes back (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A large [[sonata-form|sonata form]] movement that starts with a bold call from all three players together. Schubert introduces three themes in turn, the second making a surprising journey to a distant key. Most of the development is built on a small, tripping figure, and the movement fades out with that figure heard softly, as if from far away.

mainIdeas.name: The opening call
mainIdeas.description: all three play a strong, rising phrase together, in [[unison|unison]].

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, nodding tune that starts in E-flat minor and slides, almost by magic, into B minor.

mainIdeas.name: The tripping figure
mainIdeas.description: one longer note and four quick ones, a smaller cousin of the opening call, tossed between the instruments.

notice: Listen for the moment at ≈ 1:15 when the music slips from one minor key into another that sounds very far away. Schubert does it with a few quiet chords.

movements.heading: Andante con moto
movements.summary: Over a steady, walking accompaniment in the piano, the cello sings a sad tune in C minor taken from a Swedish song about the sunset. The tune passes from instrument to instrument, brightens for a while, then breaks out in a passionate climax before returning, quieter, at the end.

mainIdeas.name: The walk
mainIdeas.description: short, detached chords in the piano, like footsteps.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a long, sad melody in the cello, with a falling octave like a farewell; the violin and the piano take it up later.

mainIdeas.name: The climax
mainIdeas.description: the same song, loud and agitated, with the piano in full force.

stops.hear: The piano alone: short, quiet chords at a walking pace
The cello enters with a long, sad melody that falls by an octave
stops.happening: The song, based on *Se solen sjunker*

stops.hear: The tune moves to the piano, with the strings around it
Warmer, in a major key; the music opens out

notice: Follow the falling octave in the cello’s tune. It is the song’s “farewell”, and the last thing you hear.

notes.title: On film
notes.body: This movement is one of the central themes of Stanley Kubrick’s *Barry Lyndon* (1975), and has been used in many films since.

movements.heading: Scherzando. Allegro moderato
movements.summary: A light, dancing movement in three beats. It begins as a [[canon|canon]]: the piano plays a tune and the strings follow it a bar later. The middle section ([[trio|trio]]) is heavier, with stamping accents. Schubert asked for the outer part to be kept at a moderate tempo and quiet, and the middle to be forceful.

mainIdeas.name: The canon
mainIdeas.description: a neat, bouncing tune in the piano, copied by the violin and cello one bar behind.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: a heavier, stamping dance with sharp accents.

stops.hear: A light, bouncing tune in the piano; the strings repeat it a bar later
The tune slips up into a new key and the chase starts again
Heavier and louder: a stamping dance with strong accents
The light, bouncing tune again

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A quick, quiet close

notice: In the opening, try to hear the tune twice: in the piano first, then a moment later in the strings.

movements.heading: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: A long finale that mixes [[sonata-form|sonata form]] with the returning theme of a [[rondo|rondo]]. A plain, cheerful tune alternates with a second idea in a different metre, full of rapid repeated notes like a cimbalom. Twice the slow movement’s song returns, the second time over those repeated notes, before the trio ends in a bright E-flat major.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a simple, skipping tune in the piano, almost like a street song.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: the beat changes from a lilting six to a firm two, and the violin, then the piano in octaves, plays rapid repeated notes, like a cimbalom.

mainIdeas.name: The song from II
mainIdeas.description: the cello’s sad melody, back in a new setting.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The Beaux Arts Trio play the shorter version Schubert sent to the publisher, as most recordings do. His manuscript has the longer finale, with the repeat and two more passages, one of which combines the slow movement’s song with the finale’s own themes.

threads.title: The song that returns
threads.body: The Swedish sunset song of the slow movement comes back twice in the finale, an early example of [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]]. Bringing an earlier theme back in a later movement was still unusual in 1827.

threads.title: Symphonic size
threads.body: At over forty minutes, the trio is as long as many symphonies of its time, and Schubert fills it with orchestral contrasts: unison outbursts, hushed passages, long crescendos.

threads.title: Schubert and Beethoven
threads.body: He chose the anniversary of Beethoven’s death for the concert where the trio was first played in public. Beethoven, who had died the year before, was the composer he most revered.
